newsitem.title: FRANCE: France seen sticking to EMU even if left wins.
newsitem.headline: France seen sticking to EMU even if left wins.

text.p: France is expected to stick to its commitment to launch a single European currency in 1999 even if a left-wing lead in a first-round parliamentary election vote translates into victory in the second round next Sunday.

The two-round parliamentary election, called early by President Jacques Chirac to clear the way for 1999, had been presented by the ruling centre-right as a choice between launching the euro common currency on time and "shambles in Europe".

But economists believe the Socialist party, despite reservations about the direction monetary union is taking, would on balance do what it needs to do -- including making power-sharing with Chirac workable -- to get the euro launched.
"They don't have a choice," Daiwa Research Institute economist Bernard Godement said.
Among all the European countries involved in the plans to launch a single currency, France may have the most to lose if the project is abandoned.

It has put up with years of growth-choking high interest rates to maintain a link between the franc and the German mark, seen here as the linchpin of a single currency, and is only now beginning to reap the benefits of a lower cost of credit.
Giving up would be to admit the years of sacrifice, including round after round of austerity, had been in vain.

Economists nonetheless expect nervousnesss in all European financial markets next week amid fears that a Socialist government would be less likely to implement whatever austerity is needed to make France ready for Economic and Monetary Union.
"The franc is weakening. It could be negative for the lira and the peseta as well," ABN Amro economist Philippe Brossard said.

"If the second round goes the same way, it will make it much less easy to get through austerity measures and I think that this week is going to be going to be very turbulent," Nomura economist Sonja Gibbs said.

"I think other European markets will suffer as people worry about EMU uncertainties, True the Socialists have been making all the right sounds for EMU, saying yes we are for EMU, but the conditions they are attaching to France's participation in EMU are really onerous," she added.

The Socialist party set four conditions for joining a single currency -- including a flexible interpretation of the Maastricht treaty, a European "economic government", a euro which is not overvalued against the dollar and a new solidarity and growth pact to help tackle unemployment.

These conditions, however, are not that different from those of the ruling centre-right RPR-UDF coalition, and economists have stressed that both mainstream parties share a common French vision of Europe, where strong political input would balance the power of the future European central bank.
Many believe a Socialist government would compromise on Europe issues with France's other partners in the European Union, just as the centre-right did, to make a single currency possible.
"It was a Socialist administration that started Maastricht and a Conservative administration that continued it," Godement said.

Many economists also believe the Socialists would stick to sound financial management, rather than let the deficit run out of control, though Socialist leader Lionel Jospin has pledged he will not impose new austerity just to reduce the public deficit to 3.0 percent of gross domestic product.
The fact that the Socialists have called for an audit of public finances if they win power has suggested to some they are looking for an excuse for any spending squeeze which might need to be made.
And in the end Chirac will continue to control foreign policy -- and therefore European policy -- even if he has to share power with a Socialist government.
